fetched_contents.text: Gallium Nitride (GaN) Nanostructures and Their Gas Sensing Properties: A Review Abstract In the last two decades, GaN nanostructures of various forms like nanowires (NWs), nanotubes (NTs), nanofibers (NFs), nanoparticles (NPs) and nanonetworks (NNs) have been reported for gas sensing applications. In this paper, we have reviewed our group’s work and the works published by other groups on the advances in GaN nanostructures-based sensors for detection of gases such as hydrogen (H2), alcohols (R-OH), methane (CH4), benzene and its derivatives, nitric oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur-dioxide (SO2), ammonia (NH3), hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and carbon dioxide (CO2). The important sensing performance parameters like limit of detection, response/recovery time and operating temperature for different type of sensors have been summarized and tabulated to provide a thorough performance comparison. A novel metric, the product of response time and limit of detection, has been established, to quantify and compare the overall sensing performance of GaN nanostructure-based devices reported so far. According to this metric, it was found that the InGaN/GaN NW-based sensor exhibits superior overall sensing performance for H2 gas sensing, whereas the GaN/(TiO2–Pt) nanowire-nanoclusters (NWNCs)-based sensor is better for ethanol sensing. The GaN/TiO2 NWNC-based sensor is also well suited for TNT sensing. This paper has also reviewed density-functional theory (DFT)-based first principle studies on the interaction between gas molecules and GaN. The implementation of machine learning algorithms on GaN nanostructured sensors and sensor array has been analyzed as well. Finally, gas sensing mechanism on GaN nanostructure-based sensors at room temperature has been discussed. Keywords: gallium nitride (GaN), nanostructure, gas sensing, sensitivity, response/recovery time, density-functional theory (DFT), internet of things (IoT), machine learning (ML) 1. Introduction Despite having many advantages, carbon nanotubes (NTs) still suffer from the uncontrollability of selective growth of semiconducting and metallic NTs [1]. Also, the bandgap of carbon NTs cannot be controlled, hence their chemical reactivity cannot be influenced strongly [2]. Semiconducting nanowires made of compound semiconductors, possess higher flexibility as their bandgaps and doping characteristics can be tuned by manipulating the alloy composition and impurity concentrations, respectively [3]. Compound semiconductors are mainly prepared from the elements in groups II to VI of the periodic table. Several binary and ternary compound semiconductor-based nanostructure devices had been demonstrated earlier [4]. In case of group III–V compounds, each group III atom is attached to four group V atoms to achieve an octet in the valence band. The valence charge from a group V atom moves toward a group III atom and thus promotes partial ionic bonding to the crystal [5]. Bulk GaN is one of the most explored group III-nitride semiconductor materials, which has been employed in various applications such as optoelectronic devices [6], electronic devices [7], biosensors [8], chemical sensors [9,10,11] and so on. Since GaN has a direct and wide band gap of 3.4 eV at room temperature, it is quite robust. Other group III elements like Al and In can be alloyed with Ga to tune the bandgap of III-nitrides from 0.8 eV to 6 eV [12,13,14]. Moreover, it possesses high electron mobility, high heat capacity and high breakdown voltage, which are all useful properties for reliable sensing of gas/chemical molecules [15]. Internet of Things (IoT) applications require ultra-low power, mini-sized chemical sensors, which are easily integrated into electronic circuits for remote air quality monitoring in automated systems [16,17,18]. Nanostructures are suitable candidates for this type of sensing application. Having a large surface-to-volume ratio, nanostructures such as nanowires, nanorods, nanotubes, nanoparticles and nanobelts favor adsorption of gas molecules on the sensor and thus increase the sensitivity of the device [19,20,21]. The larger interaction between the gas analytes and the sensing surface allows nanostructures to be employed for high performance gas sensing as opposed to their bulk/microstructure counterparts. Although commercially available metal-oxide nanostructure-based gas sensors show high sensitivity and low detection limits [22], they suffer from issues such as poor analyte selectivity, high operating temperature and unstable performance in harsh environments [23]. GaN nanostructures offer stable operation under various radiation and in space conditions. They operate at room-temperature and can also tolerate large variations of temperature and humidity as compared to metal-oxides [24]. Thus, GaN nanostructure sensors have the potential to take over a significant share of the gas sensing market. In the past several years, efforts have been made on GaN nanostructures-based devices to detect various chemical analytes. In this work, we have reviewed our group’s work and the works published by other groups on the advances in GaN nanostructures-based sensors for detection of gases such as hydrogen (H2), alcohols (R-OH), methane (CH4), benzene and its derivatives, nitric oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur-dioxide (SO2), ammonia (NH3), hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and carbon dioxide (CO2). A novel metric, the product of response time and limit of detection, has been calculated for each sensor in order to compare the overall sensing performance. A Schottky diode based on a heterojunction of three-dimensional (3D) nanohybrid materials, formed by hybridizing reduced graphene oxide (RGO) with epitaxial vertical zinc oxide nanorods (ZnO NRs) and Al0.27GaN0.73(∼25 nm)/GaN is presented as a new class of high-performance chemical sensors. The RGO nanosheet layer coated on the ZnO NRs enables the formation of a direct Schottky contact with the AlGaN layer. The sensing results of the Schottky diode with respect to NO2, SO2, and HCHO gases exhibit high sensitivity (0.88–1.88 ppm–1), fast response (∼2 min), and good reproducibility down to 120 ppb concentration levels at room temperature. The sensing mechanism of the Schottky diode can be explained by the effective modulation of the reverse saturation current due to the change in thermionic emission carrier transport caused by ultrasensitive changes in the Schottky barrier of a van der Waals heterostructure between RGO and AlGaN layers upon interaction with gas molecules. Advances in the design of a Schottky diode gas sensor based on the heterojunction of high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas channel and highly responsive 3D-engineered sensing nanomaterials have potential not only for the enhancement of sensitivity and selectivity but also for improving operation capability at room temperature. Introduction The detection and analysis of gases are essential across a wide range of fields, including industrial safety, environmental monitoring, automotive technology, space exploration, and biomedical applications [1]. Among these, gas sensor systems play a particularly vital role in the biomedical domain, enabling the identification of specific gases that act as biomarkers for various diseases [2,3]. For instance, certain volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted by patients can serve as indicators of conditions such as diabetes or cancer, facilitating early diagnosis and timely intervention [4]. Similarly, the detection of toxic gases such as ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, and methane within the human body can assist in diagnosing gastrointestinal disorders and predicting related health conditions [5]. The development of portable gas sensor systems that balance cost-effectiveness, operational efficiency, and functional versatility is critical in addressing such urgent medical challenges [6,7]. These systems offer a promising solution by enabling precise diagnostics and real-time health monitoring in a more accessible and sustainable manner. They hold significant potential to transform healthcare delivery by making diagnostics affordable, scalable, and broadly deployable [8]. However, designing portable gas sensor systems poses two primary challenges. From a technical perspective, achieving low-power operation without compromising sensitivity and accuracy is paramount. From a commercialization standpoint, it is equally important to ensure cost-effective and robust system design. Addressing these challenges necessitates a holistic approach that includes in-depth signal analysis, the optimization of individual components, and system-level operational considerations [9,10]. To meet these demands, prior work [11] has shown that chopping large gas sensor signals into smaller components and reconstructing them via straightforward digital post-processing can effectively optimize the performance of analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) [12,13], which are traditionally among the most power-intensive and cost-constraining elements in sensor systems. A novel readout architecture is presented to efficiently process large sensor output signals while significantly easing ADC performance requirements. Moreover, a cost-efficient communication interface is implemented using a single-core microcontroller unit (MCU) [14] for real-time data handling. By analyzing the output signal patterns, the proposed method enables the use of lower-specification MCUs without sacrificing system performance, eliminating the need for high-end dual-core solutions. This reduces system complexity and the overall cost, improving scalability and applicability across diverse domains. The proposed gas sensor system addresses key limitations in portable sensor design. It preserves sensitivity while relaxing the demands on core components such as ADCs and MCUs. Through efficient signal pattern analysis, it supports real-time data handling in low-specification hardware, achieving notable reductions in power consumption and component cost. These attributes make the system highly practical and competitive particularly in biomedical applications requiring compact, low-power, and low-cost solutions. Wurtzite structure makes topmost Gallium atoms electropositive, hence high ligand binding ability especially to anions, making it usable as humidity sensor due to water self-ionization phenomenon. In this work, thin-film GaN based humidity sensor is fabricated through pulse modulated DC magnetron sputtering. Interdigitated electrodes (IDEs) with 100 μm width and spacing were inkjet printed on top of GaN sensing layer to further enhance sensor sensitivity. Impedance, capacitance, and current response were recorded for humidity and bio-sensing applications. The sensor shows approximate linear impedance response between 0 and 100% humidity range, the sensitivity of 8.53 nF/RH% and 79 kΩ/RH% for capacitance and impedance, and fast response (Tres) and recovery (Trec) time of 3.5 s and 9 s, respectively. The sensor shows little hysteresis of < 3.53% with stable and wide variations for accurate measurements. Especially, it demonstrates temperature invariance for thermal stability. Experimental results demonstrate fabricated sensor effectively evaluates plant transpiration cycle through water level monitoring by direct attachment onto leaves without causing any damage as well as freshness level of meat loaf. These properties of the proposed sensor make it a suitable candidate for future electronics providing a low-cost platform for real time monitoring applications. IoT compatibility and deployment advantages

GaN-based gas sensors are well aligned with IoT requirements because they combine small size, low power consumption, and structural robustness, all of which are critical for embedded sensing nodes. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that GaN nanostructures operate at room temperature and can tolerate large temperature and humidity variations compared to conventional metal-oxides [N1-F1]. This is important because IoT deployment often requires sensors to run in uncontrolled environments without needing constant calibration or specialized enclosures.

On the size and power side, GaN-based sensors are attractive because they can be made into compact, low-power devices. One direct example is a low-power portable gas sensor system with adaptive ROIC and Wi-Fi communication, which explicitly addresses miniaturization, low power consumption, and wireless communication for biomedical and environmental applications [N3-F3]. The same search result also states that wireless platforms for interfacing high-sensitivity nanoscale sensors are a way to improve IoT-style deployment, while another search result mentions highly miniaturized multi-parameter sensing in a single package and low power consumption of about 0.15 mA in standard mode [N3-R4]. That implies GaN-based sensing can be integrated into truly embedded IoT nodes that are small enough to fit into smart environments, wearables, or remote monitoring systems.

Wireless and edge-computing integration is another major IoT advantage. The portable system described in N3-F3 includes a single-core MCU for real-time data handling and uses a cost-efficient communication interface, which shows that GaN sensors can be paired with low-power wireless modules and edge-control logic [N3-F3]. The review evidence also notes that GaN nanostructures are suitable candidates for ultra-low-power, mini-sized chemical sensors that are easily integrated into electronic circuits for remote air quality monitoring in automated systems [N1-F1]. This makes them compatible with edge computing architectures, where sensor data is processed locally rather than sent through a centralized cloud, reducing latency and bandwidth demands.

However, there are clear trade-offs between performance and practical deployment. GaN sensors can offer high sensitivity and fast response, but those benefits may come at the cost of system complexity or power consumption if the design is not optimized. The portable system evidence explicitly states that achieving low-power operation without compromising sensitivity and accuracy is a primary technical challenge [N3-F3]. Likewise, the review notes that GaN nanostructure sensors have potential to take over a significant share of the gas-sensing market, but commercially available metal-oxide nanostructure sensors still show high sensitivity and low detection limits while suffering from poor analyte selectivity, high operating temperature, and unstable performance in harsh environments [N1-F1]. So, for IoT applications, GaN is advantageous when robustness and integration are prioritized, but designers may still need to balance sensitivity against power, size, and the need for additional conditioning electronics.

In summary, GaN-based gas sensors are especially suitable for IoT because they are compact, low-power, and compatible with wireless and edge systems, while their operational robustness reduces the need for frequent recalibration or specialized enclosures. The trade-off is that performance gains may require careful design to avoid complexity or higher power demands in practical deployments [N3-F3][N3-R4][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N9:
Limitations and practical considerations for GaN gas sensors

The main practical concerns for GaN gas sensors are environmental stability, aging effects, and commercialization bottlenecks. The evidence shows that GaN can tolerate large temperature and humidity variations compared to conventional metal-oxides, but it is not immune to environmental effects. A GaN humidity sensor study explicitly states that GaN is stable in a wide temperature range and that the sensor shows little hysteresis and stable wide variations for accurate measurements [N4-F4]. Another GaN humidity sensor paper reports a fast response and recovery time, temperature invariance, and that GaN is stable and reliable for humidity sensing [N4-R1]. However, the same review evidence also highlights that conventional metal-oxide nanostructure sensors suffer from poor selectivity, high operating temperature, and unstable performance in harsh environments, which suggests that GaN’s environmental robustness is an advantage, but real-world aging and degradation can still matter [N1-F1].

Temperature, humidity, and aging are therefore important reliability factors. The GaN humidity sensor paper states that the sensor demonstrates temperature invariance and good long-term stability, while the GaN/AlGaN heterostructure paper notes that the feasibility of GaN/AlGaN-based HEMT gas sensor devices has been demonstrated [N4-R2]. The review also emphasizes that GaN nanostructures can operate at room temperature and tolerate large variations of temperature and humidity, which is a key benefit for IoT and field deployment [N1-F1]. Still, the evidence does not indicate that GaN sensors are completely immune to aging or long-term drift; rather, it suggests that GaN-based devices are more robust than metal-oxide alternatives in harsh environments [N1-F1][N4-R3]. The humidity sensor study further reports that the GaN/Ti3C2Tx sensor shows excellent anti-humidity and good long-term stability in the 20–80% RH range, indicating that humidity resistance is achievable with appropriate design, but not automatic [N4-R3].

Current bottlenecks in commercialization and scalability include fabrication complexity, system integration, and the need for further optimization. The GaN humidity sensor fabrication paper describes a thin-film GaN humidity sensor fabricated through pulse-modulated DC magnetron sputtering with interdigitated electrodes, showing that advanced deposition techniques can produce functional sensors [N4-F4]. This points to scalability challenges: while GaN can be deposited with PMS to achieve high purity, uniformity, and adhesion, the process is not trivial and may be harder to scale than simpler metal-oxide methods [N4-F4]. The review also notes that GaN nanostructures are promising, but commercialization depends on system-level integration and optimization [N1-F1]. In other words, GaN’s material advantages do not automatically translate into low-cost, mass-producible sensor systems without careful engineering of the entire sensing platform.

As for which IoT scenarios are most and least suitable, the evidence suggests that GaN is especially well-suited for harsh or remote environments where temperature and humidity can vary widely, and where low-power, wireless integration is valuable. The humidity sensor applications described in the evidence are directly relevant to environmental monitoring, agriculture, and biomedical settings [N4-F4][N4-R1]. Conversely, scenarios requiring extremely high sensitivity at very low power or requiring ultra-low-cost mass production may still favor conventional metal-oxide sensors if the system can tolerate higher operating temperatures or lower environmental robustness [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The trade-off is that GaN excels in stability and integration-friendly operation, but may not yet be the lowest-cost option for every possible IoT use case [N1-F1][N3-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Evidence on commercialization and deployment readiness

There is evidence that GaN-based sensors are already moving toward commercial or prototype systems, though the examples are still prototype or proof-of-concept in nature. One direct example is the low-power portable gas sensor system with adaptive ROIC and Wi-Fi communication, which was developed for biomedical and environmental applications and was prototyped and evaluated at the module level [N3-F3]. Another example is the GaN humidity sensor fabricated through pulse-modulated DC magnetron sputtering, which is described as a highly stable and reliable humidity sensor suitable for real-time monitoring applications [N4-F4]. These examples show that GaN-based sensing is not just theoretical; it has reached the stage where functional prototypes are being built and tested.

Barriers to mass production and system-level integration include fabrication complexity, cost, and the need to integrate with wireless and edge-control systems. The GaN humidity sensor paper emphasizes that GaN is difficult to grow using conventional methods and that sputtering processes must be carefully controlled to achieve high-quality thin films [N4-F4]. The review likewise states that GaN nanostructure sensors are promising but that commercialization depends on system-level integration and optimization [N1-F1]. This implies that while GaN itself has favorable material properties, scaling it into high-volume sensors requires reliable deposition, electrode integration, and compatibility with standard electronics packaging. The portable gas sensor system evidence also shows that system-level constraints such as communication interfaces, power consumption, and MCU selection are important; the system uses a single-core MCU to reduce complexity and cost while still supporting Wi-Fi communication [N3-F3]. This suggests that one barrier is not just making the sensor material, but also building a complete low-power, wireless, and cost-efficient system around it.

Readiness affects IoT adoption across use cases by making some applications more practical than others. The evidence indicates that GaN-based sensors are especially attractive for biomedical and environmental monitoring because they support low power, wireless communication, and compact packaging [N3-F3][N4-F4]. The review also notes that GaN nanostructures are suitable for IoT-style sensing because they can be made into ultra-low-power, mini-sized chemical sensors that are easily integrated into electronic circuits for remote air quality monitoring in automated systems [N1-F1]. However, the same review warns that commercially available metal-oxide nanostructure sensors still show high sensitivity and low detection limits, even though they suffer from poor selectivity, high operating temperature, and unstable performance in harsh environments [N1-F1]. This means that GaN readiness is strongest in scenarios where environmental robustness and integration are priorities, but adoption may lag in applications where cost or system simplicity are the dominant constraints.

Overall, the evidence supports a picture of GaN-based sensors as commercially viable in prototype and early-deployment form, but not yet fully mature as a standardized mass-produced product. The main readiness-related issues are fabrication scalability, system integration, and the balance between performance and practical deployment constraints [N3-F3][N4-F4][N1-F1].
node_outputs.N7:
Core material and sensing advantages of GaN-based sensors

GaN’s bandgap and surface chemistry are central to its sensing advantages. The review explicitly states that GaN has a direct and wide bandgap of 3.4 eV at room temperature, making it robust and suitable for high-voltage and temperature operations [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that GaN has high electron mobility, high heat capacity, and high breakdown voltage, all of which are useful properties for reliable sensing of gas/chemical molecules [N1-F1]. Surface chemistry is also important: the GaN humidity sensor paper explains that GaN’s Wurtzite structure makes the outermost Ga atoms electropositive, giving them high ligand-binding ability, especially to anions, and enabling water self-ionization as the sensing mechanism [N4-F4]. This indicates that GaN’s surface can actively interact with target molecules rather than merely passively responding to changes in conductivity, which helps improve sensitivity and selectivity.

Selectivity and sensitivity are supported by both direct sensing mechanisms and material properties. The review notes that GaN nanostructures have a large surface-to-volume ratio, which favors adsorption of gas molecules and increases sensitivity [N1-F1]. It also states that GaN-based sensors can show stable performances over long periods, which is important for selectivity because it reduces drift and false positives [N1-F1]. The humidity sensor evidence further reports excellent anti-humidity and long-term stability, as well as a fast response and recovery time, which together support the idea that GaN can maintain consistent selectivity across repeated measurements [N4-R3][N4-F4]. In addition, the BGaN/GaN superlattice paper states that the BGaN layer increases surface trap density and trap depth, improving responsivity and high-temperature stability while also enhancing sensitivity [N1-R3]. This directly connects material engineering to improved sensing performance.
